North Macedonia remains stalled on its EU path after 21 years as a candidate
articles.summary: But North Macedonia , an EU candidate since 2005, remains stalled on the road to accession
articles.body: The European Union 's enlargement drive has regained momentum: Montenegro could become the bloc's 28th member in 2028 , while Albania is rapidly advancing through accession talks and could complete accession negotiations by the end of 2027 if it maintains its current pace of reforms. But North Macedonia , an EU candidate since 2005, remains stalled on the road to accession . That contrast will be particularly evident at Wednesday's EU- Western Balkans summit in Brussels. "The Western Balkans ' future is in the European Union. Their accession is our priority, our shared ambition and a crucial geopolitical investment in these turbulent times," European Council President Antonio Costa said ahead of the meeting. North Macedonia formally opened accession talks with the EU in July 2022 but has yet to open the first of the EU's six negotiating clusters, the groups of policy areas through which candidates align their laws and institutions with EU standards. But the lack of movement does not mean the country is unprepared for membership. EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos said in November that North Macedonia was "among the countries with the highest level of preparedness" in aligning with EU law and had recently accelerated reforms under the EU Growth Plan. Kos said that to release this handbrake and open the first cluster, North Macedonia must adopt the constitutional amendment agreed with the EU in 2022. For years, a dispute with Greece over the country's name blocked North Macedonia's progress along the EU accession path. Although the 2018 Prespa Agreement resolved the dispute, and the country changed its constitutional name, clearing the way for NATO membership, a breakthrough on EU accession did not follow. Bulgaria later blocked the process amid disputes over history, language and identity. A compromise brokered during the French EU presidency in 2022 lifted the veto but made further progress conditional on North Macedonia amending its constitution to explicitly include Bulgarians among the country's recognized communities. The amendment requires a two-thirds majority in parliament, which has so far proved unattainable. From the EU's perspective, this is no longer a Bulgarian veto, but a condition North Macedonia accepted as part of its negotiating framework. "It [North Macedonia] is not blocked by a member state. It is blocked because it doesn't want to date to do what it knows needs to be done," Gert Jan Koopman, the European Commission 's director-general for Neighbourhood and Enlargement Negotiations, recently told an Atlantic Council podcast. EU membership remains its declared strategic goal, but Skopje wants guarantees that amending its constitution will not simply pave the way for further demands from Sofia. Those concerns are rooted partly in long-running disputes over identity and history : Bulgarian governments have challenged North Macedonia's interpretation of a centuries-old distinct Macedonian identity, while some Bulgarian politicians have gone further, describing Macedonian as a regional variant of Bulgarian, and Macedonians and Bulgarians as one people. President Gordana Siljanovska-Davkova says North Macedonia is ready for talks with Bulgaria and the EU but wants certainty that one constitutional change will not simply be followed by demands for another. "We only want certainty. We only want this not to be yet another amendment for the sake of an amendment, followed by another one," she said. After more than two decades of waiting, the deadlock has also become a domestic political problem in North Macedonia. A nationally representative survey by the Institute for Democracy "Societas Civilis" illustrates the contradiction: 71% of respondents support EU membership, but only 24% back the constitutional amendments needed to advance the process. Among ethnic Macedonians, support for the amendments falls to just 11%. Skopje-based political analyst Petar Arsovski describes the public mood as "passive-aggressive:" Strong support for joining the EU coexists with weak support for making the concession currently required to move forward. The dispute is now deeply embedded in domestic politics in both North Macedonia and Bulgaria, where retreat from established positions could easily be portrayed as a national defeat. The political cost is particularly high in Skopje, where the current government came to power in part on a platform of opposition to constitutional changes under the existing conditions. For North Macedonia's government, accepting the amendments without further guarantees carries considerable domestic political risks. The uncertainty is compounded by debate over how future EU enlargement should work. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron have proposed allowing candidates to gradually gain some benefits of membership before formally joining, while stressing that full membership remains the ultimate goal. According to Arsovski, uncertainty over the future course of enlargement gives ammunition to Eurosceptic narratives and reduces the political incentive for a difficult compromise. "If these overall conditions remain unchanged, the most likely scenario is that EU summits come and go, while political actors remain dug in, with no real convergence of positions and no genuine commitment to a substantive compromise," Arsovski told DW.

articles.title: Zelenskyy calls for talks with Russia 'as soon as possible'
articles.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called on Monday for fresh four-way negotiations with Russia to begin as soon as possible
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called on Monday for fresh four-way negotiations with Russia – and involving European countries – to begin as soon as possible.

"We must do everything to make sure that the four-party meeting – Ukraine, Europe, America and Russia – happens as soon as possible," he told the 72nd NATO Parliamentary Assembly in Berlin via video link.

"We have heard from our partners that they want to try to make it happen before Christmas," he said. "We hope it happens sooner. We are ready to do this literally tomorrow."

articles.title: UN calls for investigation into attack on Russian ship off Libya
articles.body:
The UN Support Mission in Libya (UNSMIL) has expressed concern over the Ukrainian attack that sunk a Russian ship off the coast of Libya, saying in a post on X: "Libya’s sovereignty, territorial integrity and the security of its citizens and assets must be fully respected."

"UNSMIL calls for an immediate, independent and transparent investigation to establish the facts and hold those responsible to account," it added.

Libya has been split between two competing powers claiming to be the sovereign government of the country for several years.

"UNSMIL calls on all actors to act responsibly to preserve the country’s stability and build on the hard-won gains in the political process towards a durable settlement," the statement said.

articles.title: Tajikistan moves to leave ICC amid US push against court
articles.summary: Tajikistan is the fourth country to begin the withdrawal process since the United States urged countries in July to leave the court
articles.body: The governing body of the International Criminal Court (ICC) has expressed concern after Tajikistan formally notified the United Nations of its decision to withdraw from the tribunal. Tajikistan is the fourth country to begin the withdrawal process since the United States urged countries in July to leave the court. It follows Venezuela, Chad and Naoero, the Pacific island nation formerly known as Nauru. Tajikistan’s withdrawal from the Rome Statute, the treaty that established the court, is due to take effect on November 20, 2027. The ICC prosecutes individuals for genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes and the crime of aggression when national courts are unwilling or unable to act. Its 2024 arrest warrants for Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defence Minister Yoav Gallant over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza remain outstanding. The administration of US President Donald Trump has sanctioned ICC judges and prosecutors as part of its pushback against the warrants for Israeli officials and an earlier investigation into the conduct of US forces in Afghanistan. In July, the US State Department said it would seek to disable the court’s operations, portraying it as an enforcement arm of a “globalist bureaucracy” and accusing it of threatening US sovereignty. In March, the ICC found that Tajikistan had failed to comply with its request to arrest Russian President Vladimir Putin during his visit in 2025. Putin is wanted by the court over alleged war crimes in Ukraine. Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger also announced their intention to leave in 2025, denouncing the court as an instrument of “neocolonial repression”. They formally notified the UN in June, before Washington launched its campaign. Withdrawal from the ICC was part of their joint announcement. The ICC’s 125 member states still include all seven countries whose withdrawals are pending. The United States, Russia, China, Israel and India are among the nations that are not ICC member states.

articles.title: Iran exporting oil as part of undisclosed war strategy, petroleum minister says
articles.summary: Iran’s acting petroleum minister says the country has “seen a 10 percent increase in gasoline production” and continues to export petroleum products
articles.body:
Iran’s acting petroleum minister says the country has “seen a 10 percent increase in gasoline production” and continues to export petroleum products, including diesel.

Iran’s semi-official Fars news agency quoted Hamid Bovard as saying that Iran was selling oil as part of its war strategy “and we don’t disclose these things to the media”.

“We are doing our job. We are at war,” Bovard said, adding that Iran’s oil production is stable.

“Good progress has been made in the gasoline sector, and the production and consumption figures are now very close.”

articles.title: Yemen’s army says 122 Houthis killed or injured across various fronts
articles.body:
The forces of Yemen’s internationally recognised government say the Houthis have fired a ballistic missile at a house in the village of Kahlan in the governorate of Taiz, killing two civilians and injuring seven others.

In a post on X, spokesman Majed al-Nuzaili said a woman was also shot by a suspected Houthi sniper in the same area.

He said Yemen’s government forces have killed or injured at least 122 Houthi commanders and fighters in 647 targeted operations, including 545 artillery strikes, in recent hours in Marib and Taiz governorates as part of the “Dawn of Yemen” offensive launched in early October.

articles.title: Russia’s Medvedev blames ‘double standards’ for US war on Iran
articles.body:
Former Russian President Dmitry Medvedev, currently deputy chairman of Russia’s Security Council, has questioned the United States over its attacks on Iran and the justifications used for the war.

In an article published on Monday, Medvedev said the US decision to launch the war alongside Israel under the pretext of defending global nuclear nonproliferation – despite Iran’s repeated commitment to it – reflects “double standards” and a hidden agenda.

Iran has long been a signatory to the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT) and has denied building nuclear weapons.

Following US and Israeli attacks on Iran’s main nuclear facilities and assassinations of senior leaders and scientists, Iranian authorities have increasingly discussed the possibility of abandoning the international treaty and building an atomic bomb.

articles.title: Flights cancelled in Belgium due to cost-of-living strike
articles.summary: Underground services have also been halted in capital Brussels, where large numbers of people joined a protest march
articles.body: A few people have turned up at Brussels airport where no flights are leaving Hundreds of flights have been cancelled and public transport severely disrupted across Belgium as a result of a strike against planned austerity measures. All air traffic has been halted at Brussels Airport in Zaventem as well as at Charleroi, home to low-cost airlines such as Ryanair. Underground services have also been halted in capital Brussels, where large numbers of people joined a protest march. The protest comes as Prime Minister Bart De Wever continues talks with his coalition allies over a budget to cut borrowing costs. King Philippe declined his resignation earlier this month, giving De Wever more time to negotiate. No flights are taking off or landing at Brussels Airport between 07:00 and 21:00 local time (06:00-20:00 GMT) as a result of the strike by air traffic controllers. "In total, 404 flights today cannot be operated, which has an impact on more than 50,000 passengers," Brussels Airport spokesperson Jeffrey Franssens said. Reuters news agency spoke to Florence Faure, a French passenger who had arrived in Brussels from China's capital, Beijing, only to find that her flight to Paris Charles de Gaulle airport had been cancelled. "Since our luggage was supposed to go on to Paris Charles de Gaulle, we didn't even collect it," she said. A similar situation has affected Charleroi, where all flights were shown as "scheduled", regardless of the time of departure or arrival. One passenger told Belgian broadcaster RTBF that she had received no warning and only discovered there were no flights when she arrived at the airport. Philippe Naime, a teacher, was one of the tens of thousands taking part in the protest march in Brussels. "Quite simply, no more money is being invested in education, and people are left to fend for themselves. But people do not have the means to do that," he told Reuters. Public transport, schools and other public services are also facing disruptions. Large numbers of people have descended on Brussels for a protest march One of its members, the socialist Vooruit, has been refusing to endorse plans agreed by the other four. It wants to raise taxes on the rich and for there to be fewer cuts to pensions and the health sector. De Wever met King Philippe on Monday for the third update since the impasse. "While expressing regret over the lack of significant progress, the king encouraged the prime minister to persevere in order to reach an agreement as soon as possible," the royal palace said in a statement. The leader of one of the country's main unions, FGTB, said the government had alternatives to "dismantling the social protection system". Bert Engelaar, head of the union, called for "a genuine wealth tax, fair taxation, and the elimination of tax loopholes". "Political responsibility is not about keeping a government afloat at all costs. It's about knowing when to stop," he added, praising the Vooruit party. Another union leader, Ann Vermorgen of the CSC, criticised government plans to cut bank holidays when they fall on weekends.

Reports: Russia planning to station nuclear weapon in space
articles.body:
Western military intelligence services believe Russia is planning to station a nuclear weapon in space by the end of this year, German media reported on Monday morning.

According to public broadcasters NDR and WDR, as well as the Süddeutsche Zeitung broadsheet, intelligence chiefs believe Moscow intends to fire a satellite armed with a nuclear warhead into orbit.

Intelligence regarding the plans was reportedly shared among NATO member states recently and German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius is said to have been informed by experts from Germany's armed forces, the Bundeswehr.

A Bundeswehr spokesman reportedly declined to comment on the reports, acknowledging only that Russia does possess such capabilities and warning that a nuclear explosion in space would have devastating consequences for global satellite communications.

"It would effectively mean: back to the stone age," he said.

The German Ministry of Defense said only that it was continuously observing global developments in space while the Russian embassy in Berlin said it had no information regarding such plans.

The United States Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA) warned in October that Russia was developing a satellite capable of transporting a nuclear weapon and, according to the new report, a satellite codenamed "Sputnik-S" is believed to have been in storage in the Moscow area for several years.

Back in February 2022, the same month as the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Russia launched its "Kosmos-2552" satellite into orbit, considered by western intelligence at the time to be a test designed to measure the effects of radiation in space.

Should Moscow indeed launch a nuclear weapon into space, it would constitute a breach of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty which prohibits the stationing of weapons of mass destructions in Earth orbit. Russia agreed to a continuation of the treaty at the United Nations General Assembly in December 2024.

Space is nevertheless becoming increasingly militarized, with the United States admitting in September 2025 that it had positioned offensive non-nuclear weapons in orbit.

articles.title: Oil refinery in southern Russia suspends operations after attack
articles.body:
The ‌Novoshakhtinsk in the Russian state of Rostov has suspended its operations after a barrage of attacks overnight, the state governort Yuri Slyusar said on Telegram.

Slyusar said the attack, which involved both drones and missiles, lasted over six hours.

He added that emergency services were working to contain the aftermath.

Ukraine has repeatedly targeted Russian refineries as a means to hamper the Russian economy.

The Novoshakhtinsk refinery lies close to Ukraine's eastern border with Russia. It mainly refines oil for export and has a capacity of 100,000 barrels per day.

articles.title: Ukrainian attack kills 1 in Russia's Perm, governor says
articles.body:
The governor of Russia's Perm region, Dmitry Makhonin, said one person was killed in a Ukrainian drone attack that hit and damaged several industrial sites.

Two others were injured by shrapnel, Makhonin said in a post on Telegram.

The governor said 56 drones had been shot down. It wasn't clear how many drones were involved in the attack.

Perm lies some 1,700 km (1,050 miles) from Ukrainian-held territory and is home to an oil refinery that has repeatedly come under attack.

articles.title: Anti-austerity strike spurs transport chaos across Belgium
articles.summary: Air traffic was also halted on Monday at Brussels’ Charleroi airport, which is used by low-cost airlines such as Ryanair
articles.body: Transport services across Belgium have been disrupted, with hundreds of flights and trains cancelled , as trade unions called a national strike to protest against the federal government’s austerity measures. Monday’s walkout grounded planes across the country after air traffic controller Skeyes said it was unable to provide regular services at Belgian airports. In a statement on its website, Brussels airport said that “unfortunately, all departing and arriving flights from 7am to 9pm local time (06:00-20:00 GMT) will have to be cancelled”. Air traffic was also halted on Monday at Brussels’ Charleroi airport, which is used by low-cost airlines such as Ryanair. The Board of Airline Representatives in Belgium, which represents about 25 carriers, said the strike would be the 11th affecting Belgian airspace in as many months. The national strike has also caused disruption to buses, trains, schools, and other public services. Belgium has faced repeated cost-of-living protests and strikes in recent months, with much of the anger directed towards Prime Minister Bart De Wever and his attempts at cost-cutting. The Belgian government is trying to save 10 billion euros ($10.9bn) in the coming years to reduce the country’s high deficit, but the issue is dividing the ruling coalition and threatens to collapse the government. De Wever has already offered King Philippe his resignation, but the monarch refused to accept it, giving him more time to find a solution to the budget impasse. The prime minister has now set a new December 31 ⁠ ⁠⁠ ⁠deadline for his government to reach an agreement on next year’s budget, ⁠⁠⁠⁠after another week of talks ended without a result. “Should we not have a budget agreement [before the end of the year], the ‌‌‌‌government will effectively be unable to govern, thereby bringing its existence to an end”, De Wever’s office said in a statement. The government is looking at spending cuts, notably in healthcare, and a VAT increase to bring down the deficit, but unions have been pushing for taxes on high earners to offset some of the cuts, as protests against rising living costs continue, not only in Belgium but across Europe .

articles.summary: The text of the document has been published on the official website of the President of Azerbaijan
articles.body: BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 23. Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev has signed an order on the conscription of citizens for compulsory active military service and the transfer of servicemen completing their compulsory service to the reserve from January 1 through 30, 2027. The text of the document has been published on the official website of the President of Azerbaijan. Under the order, citizens of Azerbaijan born in 2009 who have reached the age of 18 by the date of conscription (inclusive), as well as those born between 1997 and 2008 who are under the age of 30, have not completed compulsory active military service in the Azerbaijani Armed Forces, and are not entitled to deferment or exemption from conscription, will be called up for compulsory active military service from January 1 through 30, 2027. Servicemen who have completed the service period stipulated in Article 38.1.1 of the Law of the Republic of Azerbaijan "On Military Duty and Military Service" will be transferred to the reserve from January 1 through 30, 2027. The Cabinet of Ministers of Azerbaijan is tasked with taking the measures provided for by law to implement this order.

articles.title: Ademovic: The Constitutional Court of BiH is the only bulwark against the Secessionist Policy of the RS
articles.summary: This assessment was offered by Nedim Ademović—a lawyer and expert in constitutional law—during the Dnevnik 2 news program on Federal Television
articles.body: The Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina remains the only state-level institution with the capacity to halt actions that threaten the sovereignty, independence, and functionality of the state. This assessment was offered by Nedim Ademović—a lawyer and expert in constitutional law—during the Dnevnik 2 news program on Federal Television. He was commenting on recent rulings by the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina, political rhetoric emanating from the Republika Srpska (RS), and announcements that the formation of government at the state level would be made conditional upon certain demands. Ademović warns that the Constitutional Court is currently under fire precisely because of its role in upholding the constitutional order, and that any potential reforms aimed at limiting its functionality would pose a serious risk to Bosnia and Herzegovina. He argues that pro-Bosnian political forces must begin considering various scenarios now and focus on safeguarding the institutional capacity of this body. Constitutional Court Rulings on the Commission and Symbols of the Army of the RBiH Were Expected Addressing the Constitutional Court’s rulings—which concerned a veto exercised by Željka Cvijanović regarding the Commission to Preserve National Monuments, as well as an attempt to criminalize the display of symbols associated with the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina—Ademović characterized these actions by the authorities in the Republika Srpska as unconstitutional. “In my view, these are blatantly unconstitutional acts by the RS, which continue to attempt to weaken the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina, its institutions, and its functionality. These rulings are significant because such acts are being eliminated from the constitutional and legal framework of our state. Nevertheless, given that these are blatantly unconstitutional decisions, they were the only ones to be expected,” said Ademović. He pointed out that the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina has demonstrated that it is the only state institution capable of functioning independently and halting moves that threaten the sovereignty and independence of the state. Explaining the decision regarding the Commission to Preserve National Monuments of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Ademović stated that the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina had adopted the decision to appoint members of the Commission by a majority vote; however, Željka Cvijanović attempted to invoke an “entity veto”—facilitated by the National Assembly of Republika Srpska—to overturn it. “The Constitutional Court ruled that this was not permissible, for the simple reason that an entity veto cannot be used indiscriminately; it may only be applied in relation to five specific competencies defined by the Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The ruling is logical and straightforward. It now paves the way for this vital commission to finally become functional again, after so many years,” Ademović clarified. Commenting on a statement by Savo Minić—a representative of Republika Srpska—that a state-level government cannot be formed without first resolving issues concerning the Office of the High Representative (OHR), state property, and the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Ademović highlighted the Court’s critical role in upholding the constitutional order. “For Republika Srpska – on its radical, secessionist path – the Constitutional Court stands as the sole institution that truly serves as a bulwark against such a policy. Unlike other institutions – such as the state-level legislative body or the Council of Ministers – the Constitutional Court is not subject to vetoes, ethnic quotas, or specific majority requirements. Instead, it reaches decisions by a simple majority vote, just like any other court in Europe,” said Ademović. He added that this is the only institution with the capacity to declare certain acts unconstitutional – a step that, as he noted, opens the door for the international community to take action, including political and other measures, to halt the moves made by the authorities of the Republika Srpska (RS). “I still believe that the RS, as an entity, is stronger than Bosnia and Herzegovina in terms of de facto power. However, without the Constitutional Court, they might be able to exercise that de facto power. With the Constitutional Court in place, that is impossible, because there is always a document on the table that spells out what they are doing right and what they are doing wrong,” Ademović pointed out. According to him, it is precisely for this reason that the RS authorities are seeking to reform the Constitutional Court in a way that would render it dysfunctional – mirroring the blocking mechanisms already present in other state institutions. Warning Regarding Potential Reforms Reflecting on the international landscape and the efforts of the Republika Srpska (RS) authorities to achieve their political objectives, Ademović pointed to the passivity of the European Union, as well as shifts in international relations. “Global circumstances – specifically the relationship with the United States and the RS’s active engagement with that country, the passivity of the European Union (another key player), and the situation in our immediate neighborhood – are currently not particularly conducive to upholding the functionality and prosperity of Bosnia and Herzegovina,” Ademović assessed. He believes it is time to sound the alarm, noting that key reforms in Bosnia and Herzegovina since the Dayton Peace Agreement came into effect have largely been the result of international community involvement or pressure exerted on domestic political actors by third parties. He warned that, under these conditions, room could open up for a compromise involving the reform of the Constitutional Court – a move that would undermine its functionality. “Circumstances could align in such a way that pressure is applied once again, leading to concessions – specifically, a compromise involving the reform of the Constitutional Court. We must be extremely cautious here. The Constitutional Court, as a functional institution that defends this state, must remain functional – exactly as it is. We must not allow the introduction of elements that have compromised other institutions in Bosnia and Herzegovina—such as requirements for the mandatory presence of a specific number of representatives from certain ethnic groups to establish a quorum or make decisions,” Ademović stated. He concluded that pro-Bosnian forces face a serious task and must begin developing possible options for a potential reform of the Constitutional Court – ensuring, however, that the institution retains the functionality and capacities it possesses today, Federalna writes.

articles.title: Constitutional Court of BiH: Republika Srpska Can’t Ban the Insignia of the Army of RBiH
articles.summary: The challenged provision of Article 359b of the Criminal Code of Bosnia and Herzegovina (Official Gazette of Republika Srpska Nos
articles.body: At the session, the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina ruled that the provision of the Criminal Code of Republika Srpska, which criminalizes the display and glorification of the symbols, the flag and the insignia of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, is unconstitutional! Among other things, the Court confirmed that its insignia belong to the military heritage of the Armed Forces of BiH and that their use is grounded in valid state regulations. “In this case, the Constitutional Court decided on the requests of eleven members of the House of Representatives of the Parliamentary Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Denis Bećirović, at the time of submitting a request, Chairman of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Denis Zvizdić, at the time of submitting a request, the First Deputy Chair of the House of Representatives of the Parliamentary Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, for a review of the constitutionality of Article 359b of the Criminal Code of Republika Srpska. The challenged provision of Article 359b of the Criminal Code of Bosnia and Herzegovina (Official Gazette of Republika Srpska Nos. 64/17, 104/18 – Constitutional Court of RS Decision, 15/21, 89/21, http://www.ohr.int – High Representative Decision No. 12/23, ‘Official Gazette of Republika Srpska’ No. 73/23, ‘Official Gazette of BiH’ No. 9/24 – Constitutional Court of BiH Decision, ‘Official Gazette of Republika Srpska’ Nos. 105/24 – Constitutional Court of RS Decision, 19/25, 31/25, ‘Official Gazette of BiH’ No. 36/25 – Constitutional Court of BiH Decision, ‘Official Gazette of Republika Srpska’ Nos. 85/25 – Constitutional Court of RS Decision, 92/25 – Law on the Cessation of Validity of Laws, 25/26, and 78/26) criminalized the public display, showing, production, reproduction, or in any way putting into circulation of flags, symbols, insignia, greetings, or slogans that promote or glorify the Army of RBiH. The Constitutional Court concluded that the provision of Article 359 b of the Criminal Code of Republika Srpska is not in line with Articles I(2) and III(3)(b) of the Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In its reasoning for the decision, the Constitutional Court, among other things, emphasized that the challenged provision is not aligned with the laws regarding the use of official symbols and insignia of the Army of RBiH. The regulations of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina regarding the appearance and the use of symbols and insignia of the Army of RBiH continue to apply on the territory of BiH based on the constitutional principle of continuity approved by Article I(1) of the Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in conjunction with Article 2 of Annex II to the Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The National Assembly has no jurisdiction to decide on the cessation of validity of legal acts of the institutions of RBiH, whose continuity is constitutionally recognized. The challenged provision is therefore not aligned with Article III (3)(b) of the Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in light of the continuity of legal provisions, as it disrupts the normative hierarchy which the Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina unequivocally established in Article III (3) (b) through the harmonization of legal regulations within the legal systems according to their hierarchy, in which state laws must be aligned with the decisions of the institutions of BiH. In addition to this, pursuant to the decisions of the institutions of BiH, the Army of RBiH is part of the Armed Forces of BiH with its military heritage and identity, along with recognizable insignia, the display of which constitutes a duty for the respective infantry regiments. Therefore, the challenged provision is not aligned with Article I(2) of the Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina because it violates the decisions of the institutions of BiH requiring members of the regiment to wear their regimental insignia.”

Albania's Foreign and Defence Ministries deny any role in attack on Russian warship in Libya
articles.summary: According to media reports, it was carried out by Ukraine's intelligence services
articles.body: The Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs and the Ministry of Defence have rejected claims that the drone attack on a Russian warship in Benghazi, Libya, was planned or launched from Albanian territory. The attack happened on Sunday morning. According to media reports, it was carried out by Ukraine's intelligence services. It drew wide attention because it took place far from the front line and in another country, taking the war beyond the borders of Ukraine and Russia. On Sunday evening, a platform that covers military affairs and armed conflicts wrote that the Ukrainian drones had been launched from Albania. That claim pulled Albania into the story, alongside Russia and Ukraine, which have been at war since 2022, and Libya, where the attack took place. In their official responses, both ministries denied any Albanian involvement. They described the reports as inaccurate and not backed by evidence. The Foreign Ministry said the claims that the attack was launched from Albania "do not reflect the facts." "Albania was not involved in this incident, and its territory was not used or made available to launch or support such an attack," the ministry said in a statement. The ministry firmly rejected the accusations. It asked the media and platforms that published them to correct their reports and to stop presenting unverified claims as fact. The Ministry of Defence also denied that Albania's armed forces played any part in the operation. "The Armed Forces of the Republic of Albania did not carry out, take part in, or provide any support for such an operation," it said. The ministry stressed the difference between the fact that an attack happened and the claim that it was launched from Albania. "The fact that an attack took place does not prove where the weapons came from, let alone that Albania was involved," the ministry said. It warned that publishing such claims without independent checks risks spreading a false story linking Albania to a military operation against Russia. A Russian Navy corvette, first identified as the Merkury, caught fire after a powerful explosion at the naval base in Benghazi, in eastern Libya, in the early hours of Sunday, November 22, 2026. The ship has been identified as a Project 20380 Steregushchiy-class missile corvette. According to reports, it had come to Benghazi to take on fuel and supplies as part of cooperation between Russia and the authorities in eastern Libya. Sources quoted by Al Jazeera said there were Russian and Libyan casualties, but gave no confirmed numbers. The ship sank. Photos taken after the incident show only part of it above the water. Witnesses quoted by Al Jazeera said they saw three drones during the night attack. Sources cited by the Associated Press said the drones had been launched from a Ukrainian-controlled base in western Libya. Authorities in Benghazi have opened a joint investigation with Russia. So far they have not directly blamed Ukraine, but they have said that Libya is not a party to the war between Russia and Ukraine. At the time of reporting, no one had officially claimed responsibility for the attack. The claim that the attack came from Albania was first published by Clash Report. In a post on X, the platform said that, according to one of its sources, the drones used to hit the Russian warship had been launched from Albania, not from western Libya. The post also claimed that eastern Libyan authorities had identified where the drones were launched from, and that the western Libya story was a cover put out by Ukrainian sources. However, Clash Report did not name its source and did not publish any evidence that the drones came from Albania. According to the Ministry of Defence, the claim was later repeated by another platform, Visioner, which reported that the drones had travelled more than 800 kilometres across the Mediterranean. The ministry said the report was not backed by evidence and warned against repeating it as confirmed fact. Clash Report is a platform that publishes news about military conflicts and international security. It has more than 850,000 followers on X. According to an investigation by researcher Eitan Fischberger, the platform is linked to the Turkish company Monolog Medya, which is run by a former executive of Turkish state broadcaster TRT. Media Bias/Fact Check rates the platform's factual reliability as "mixed." In the Benghazi case, the claim about Albania was published without naming a source and without any independent evidence about where the drones came from.

articles.summary: Ruling Democratic Party of Korea (DPK) Chairman Kim Min-seok, center, listens as Rep
articles.body: Ruling Democratic Party of Korea (DPK) Chairman Kim Min-seok, center, listens as Rep. Choi Min-hee, left, a member of the DPK's supreme Council, speaks during a council meeting at the National Assembly in Yeouido, Seoul, Monday. Yonhap Ruling Democratic Party of Korea (DPK) Chairman Kim Min-seok heads into his 100th day in office on Tuesday, as party support slips amid a deepening factional feud, in stark contrast to the turnaround he promised. Kim pledged during his leadership campaign to raise the DPK’s support by at least 10 percentage points within three months. But a Gallup Korea poll released on Friday put the DPK’s support at 36 percent, down from 41 percent in a survey conducted from Aug. 11–13, just before Kim took office on Aug. 17. Under the circumstances, Kim’s leadership will face another test as he tries to reunite the DPK and win over centrist voters while the party’s hard-liners push to impeach Supreme Court Chief Justice Cho Hee-dae — a move that could rally its base and alienate moderates. “It appears the voters still don’t feel they can count on the ruling party to settle problems under Kim’s leadership,” said Jung Jae-hwan, a political science professor at Inha University. “The move to impeach the chief justice will test whether Kim can keep the party focused on voters’ everyday concerns while managing a dispute with the judiciary.” The impeachment push has split the party along factional lines. Hard-liners aligned with former DPK Chairman Jung Chung-rae continue to press for immediate impeachment. Kim, who defeated Jung in a bitterly contested leadership race, had initially proposed an inquiry by the National Assembly first. The party formally backed impeachment on Friday, but the two camps could still disagree over when to file the motion. The dispute stems from a Supreme Court ruling under Cho that went against President Lee Jae Myung weeks before the 2025 presidential election. The ruling overturned Lee’s acquittal on charges of making false statements during his previous presidential campaign and ordered a new trial. Shincheonji allegations The fight over Cho adds to a series of disputes that have deepened the feud since Kim took office. During the August leadership race, Kim accused Jung’s supporters of forming a secret alliance with the Shincheonji religious sect. He apologized on Nov. 3 after acknowledging he had no evidence for the claim, but Jung’s faction continued to demand that he take responsibility. Tensions flared again on Nov. 13 when three Supreme Council members aligned with Jung — Reps. Choi Min-hee, Han Min-soo and Lee Sung-yun — boycotted a leadership meeting. They protested Kim’s decision to order an ethics inquiry into Choi after a recording surfaced in which she said President Lee had opposed the impeachment of former President Yoon Suk Yeol over his botched martial law declaration in December 2024. Shin Yul, a political science professor at Myongji University, said the factional feud could hurt the DPK’s chances in the 2028 parliamentary elections if it drags on. “The ruling party candidates could go into the 2028 elections having to explain their party’s infighting instead of telling voters what they plan to do for them,” Shin said. “That could cost the party support among undecided voters, especially in closely contested districts.”

Serbia’s Student Movement Criticises European Parliament’s Vukovar Resolution
articles.summary: It argued that the draft resolution overlooks some of the suffering of Serb civilians in Croatia
articles.body: Serbia’s student movement, which under the name Student List won the country’s recent parliamentary elections, has criticised a European Parliament’s draft resolution marking the 35th anniversary of the fall of Vukovar in eastern Croatia, calling for adequate recognition of war crimes committed against Serb civilians during the Croatian conflict. In a statement on the Student List – Students Win website on Monday, it said the resolution does not contribute to an “objective understanding of historical events” or to reconciliation. It argued that the draft resolution overlooks some of the suffering of Serb civilians in Croatia, including killings, persecution and mass displacement, particularly during the Croatian military operations Flash and Storm in 1995. “Responsibility for war crimes must be individual and established on the basis of evidence and final court judgments, rather than attributed to entire nations,” the students said. “Serbia has an obligation to cooperate in clarifying the fate of missing persons and establishing responsibility for crimes committed, but the same approach must also apply to Serb victims and crimes committed against them,” the student movement said. The eastern border town of Vukovar fell to the Yugoslav People’s Army and Serb paramilitaries on November 18, 1991, during the war in Croatia, after which the remaining population was expelled. Two days after the town fell, Croatian prisoners and civilians were taken from Vukovar Hospital to a nearby farm where at least 200 people were executed. The student movement warned that remembrance of the past should not deepen existing divisions in the region. “True reconciliation cannot be achieved by imposing one-sided interpretations of the past, but through an honest reckoning with all crimes, regardless of who committed them or against whom,” they added. The European Parliament was set to debate the resolution on Monday, with a vote scheduled for Thursday. The debate in Strasbourg follows the submission of two motions for a resolution on November 20, commemorating the victims of the siege of Vukovar and the atrocities that followed. One of the motions, submitted by members of the European People’s Party, EPP, the Socialists and Democrats, S&D, the European Conservatives and Reformists, ECR, and the Greens/EFA, notes that 1,725 cases of missing persons from the war remain unresolved, including 1,341 people whose fate remains unknown and 384 whose deaths have been confirmed but whose burial sites have yet to be located. It also calls on Serbia to grant access to relevant wartime archives, disclose information about the locations of individual and mass graves, fight against impunity for war crimes and facilitate the identification and return of victims’ remains to their families. The proposal further urges Serbia to adopt its long-announced law on missing persons. The motion condemns the denial and glorification of war crimes, specifically referring to the public honours paid in Serbia to the convicted war criminal and former Bosnian Serb commander Ratko Mladic at his funeral in Belgrade in September 2026. It further calls for educational, cultural and commemorative programmes that promote a “fact-based understanding of the Croatian Homeland War and the 1990s”, while encouraging reconciliation and respect for all victims. The proposal acknowledges the work of the International Criminal Tribunal, ITCY, for the former Yugoslavia in prosecuting crimes committed in Vukovar, but adds that not all those responsible have been brought to justice. The motion also highlights the peaceful reintegration of Serb-held eastern Croatian into Croatia in 1998 as an example of successful post-war reintegration and the importance of rebuilding trust between communities.

articles.body: BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 23. According to him, one of the key points emphasized in the book is that Turkmenistan's permanent neutrality was not an arbitrary choice but has deep historical roots, is closely linked to the national traditions of the Turkmen people, and became part of the country's state policy following independence. Habibbayli noted that, alongside the sociopolitical and diplomatic dimensions of neutrality, the book examines the distinctive features of Turkmen national identity, including the people's culture, ancient Turkic monuments, family traditions, moral values and approaches to upbringing. "This book is a kind of modern passport of Turkmenistan," he emphasized, adding that the publication would be valuable to anyone interested in the country's history, culture and contemporary development. Habibbayli said that publishing the book in Azerbaijani and presenting it to a broad audience would help strengthen the friendship and fraternal ties between the peoples of Azerbaijan and Turkmenistan.

Netanyahu rival condemns ‘Jewish terrorism’ after settler attacks on Palestinian villages
articles.summary: Israeli police said they had launched an investigation with forensic teams
articles.body: Arson attacks by militant Israeli settlers on Palestinian villages in the occupied West Bank have caused a political row in Israel, drawing condemnation from Gadi Eisenkot, the opposition leader, who described them as “Jewish terrorism”. Dozens of settlers raided Palestinian communities overnight on Saturday, setting fire to about a dozen vehicles and several homes and scrawling racist graffiti. At least four communities were attacked. Israeli police said they had launched an investigation with forensic teams. Photographs from Kafr Malik , near Ramallah, showed one slogan written in Hebrew that read: “This is the first revenge.” Several vehicles and homes had been set alight in the village. Images from nearby Deir al-Sudan showed vehicles on fire. Palestinian reports said an agricultural building had been set ablaze in Deir Ballut and cars torched in Deir Abu Mashal. An ⁠inconclusive election last month stripped Benjamin Netanyahu, the prime minister, of his majority. Eisenkot has been asked to form a government, though his prospects seem little better. “Last night’s arson attacks in Judea and Samaria were acts of Jewish terrorism, in every sense of the term,” Eisenkot said, using the biblical name for the West Bank. “Extremist groups that set fire to vehicles and homes are undermining regional stability, putting lives at risk and doing grave damage to Israel’s national security and foreign relations.” Referring to the far-right ministers Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, he added: “The actions led by Ben-Gvir and Smotrich in the West Bank have brought the area to the brink of unchecked anarchy.” Eisenkot, who has been given 28 days to form a government by the president, Isaac Herzog, with a possible 14-day extension, urged the government and security establishment to “use every tool at their disposal – including administrative detention and targeted operations by the Shin Bet – to stop the rioters and impose harsh sanctions on them”. In an unprecedented rebuke on Sunday, several other members of the Israeli parliament criticised Netanyahu over escalating violence by militant settlers against Palestinians. Yair Lapid, the leader of Yesh Atid, held Netanyahu’s government responsible for encouraging the attacks. “Jewish terrorism is the product of criminal negligence by the Israeli government,” he said on X, adding that ministers were deliberately encouraging the militant settlers’ violence “through their silence”. Yair Golan, the leader of the Democrats party, warned of the possibility of a third intifada and described the West Bank as “on the brink of an explosion”. “Anyone who wants to prevent a third intifada must replace the current government, which provides cover and support for Jewish terrorism and abandons security,” Golan said on X. “Jewish terrorism harms innocent Palestinians and Israeli army soldiers, and pushes Israel toward unprecedented international isolation.” Noam Tibon, a retired army major general and Knesset member, gave a similar warning. “If Israel does not eliminate Jewish terrorism in the West Bank, it will destroy Israel,” he wrote. Australia announced sanctions on Wednesday against three people and four Israeli entities, including a construction company, over their role in the expansion of illegal settlements and human rights abuses against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank. A day earlier the UK imposed sanctions on eight Israeli construction companies involved in building illegal settlements in the West Bank, which the UN regards as Palestinian territory under Israeli occupation since 1967. Since the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attacks on Israel, there has been a surge of Israeli settlement expansion and violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank. More than 1,100 Palestinians have been killed there by Israeli forces or settlers. On Tuesday, a 72-year-old Palestinian woman was shot dead in an overnight attack by Israeli militant settlers in a village near Jericho, where the group has recently moved in after taking over several Palestinian homes.

articles.title: Ukraine 'keep finding ways to get back on our feet after every Russian attack,' Zelenskyy says
articles.summary: In the last half hour, Volodymyr Zelenskyy addressed the Nato parliamentary Assembly meeting in Berlin
articles.body:
In the last half hour, Volodymyr Zelenskyy addressed the Nato parliamentary Assembly meeting in Berlin.

He warned that “Russian aggression has shown that when Ukraine is left out, and when there is no clear understanding of how Europe should be protected, anything can happen.”

He also celebrated overnight strikes against Russia, saying Ukraine “keep finding ways to get back on our feet after every Russian attack.”

“Today, Russia can feel our response all the way from western Siberia, where its oil refiners are burning, to the coast of Libya, where its warships are sinking.”

Zelenskyy stressed that Ukraine has repeatedly offered “steps to reduce the fighting,” and “never been the ones to raise the stakes,” but Russia “still gives us no peaceful response.”

He urged Nato leaders to “invest in stronger security and greater resilience,” saying “does anyone here still believe that one day Russia will simply become peaceful and safe again?”

“Just look at the last, last 100 years of Russian history. … There is no reason to believe that Russia will become a different country in one year or five years. So we must act in a way that makes sure that no matter what kind of Russia we face and no matter what threats our countries face, we will always have enough to defend ourselves.”

He urged partners to support Ukraine ahead of winter, particularly helping with air defence systems.

“The stronger our defences are, the less chance Russia has to break through them and the more chance diplomacy has to work.”

The Ukrainian president also slightly pushed back against the suggested Article Five-like security guarantees for Ukraine in case of a peace deal with Russia, arguing that it should simply be allowed to join Nato instead.

“When we talk about Article Five-like guarantees, we need answers. We need answers to some very clear questions. Which countries will support Ukraine if Ukraine is attacked again, what exactly will our partners do in response? Which troops will be stationed on our territory in advance? How much will all these cost and will it really work? All of this is not easy and so far we have no clear, specific answers with respect to such ideas.”

articles.title: Ex-Justice Minister Kang tapped as spy agency chief
articles.summary: He said the changes would bring in new leadership to protect Korea’s interests as the international landscape shifts
articles.body: National Intelligence Service Director nominee Kang Kum-sil / Yonhap President Lee Jae Myung nominated former Justice Minister Kang Kum-sil to head the National Intelligence Service (NIS), Monday. Lee also tapped Lim Woong-soon, his second deputy national security adviser and a former ambassador to Canada, as foreign minister, and Hong Ihk-pyo, a former presidential secretary for political affairs and former floor leader of the ruling Democratic Party of Korea (DPK), as unification minister. Presidential chief of staff Lim Kwang-hyun announced the Cabinet reshuffle largely focused on the security and diplomacy sectors during a briefing at Cheong Wa Dae in Seoul. He said the changes would bring in new leadership to protect Korea’s interests as the international landscape shifts. “Kang is the most suitable person to reinforce democratic oversight of the NIS, based on her strong belief in the neutrality of powerful organizations. She is also expected to resolve new security threats, such as cyberattacks, through international cooperation,” the chief of staff said. A former Seoul High Court judge, Kang became Korea’s first female justice minister under the 2003-08 Roh Moo-hyun administration and now serves as ambassador for global climate and environment. If confirmed by the National Assembly, she would be the first woman to lead the spy agency in the history of the NIS and its predecessor agency, founded in 1961. President Lee Jae Myung nominated four Cabinet ministers Monday. From left are Foreign Minister nominee Lim Woong-soon, Unification Minister nominee Hong Ihk-pyo, Interior Minister nominee Han Jun-ho and Culture Minister nominee Kang Yu-jung. Courtesy of Cheong Wa Dae Lim Woong-soon is a career diplomat who served as a minister at the Korean Embassy in Washington and worked on North Korean nuclear issues at the foreign ministry. “Lim Woong-soon is a suitable person to build on Korea-U.S. cooperation based on the ironclad alliance,” the chief of staff said, adding that the foreign minister nominee is expected to expand the horizons of diplomacy from security and trade to industry and advanced technology. Hong, who stepped down as presidential secretary for political affairs earlier this month, previously worked at the Korea Institute for International Economic Policy and served on the National Assembly’s Foreign Affairs and Unification Committee. The chief of staff said Hong was well placed to lead efforts to ease inter-Korean tensions and rebuild trust. The reshuffle replaced Unification Minister Chung Dong-young and NIS Director Lee Jong-seok, both of whom had prioritized engagement with North Korea but were widely seen as contributing to recent frictions with Washington. There are speculations that the changes are related to fallout from Chung’s March remarks to the National Assembly identifying Kusong as the site of a North Korean uranium enrichment facility, after which the U.S. restricted some intelligence sharing on North Korea. At an October parliamentary audit, NIS Director Lee confirmed that Washington had limited information sharing, citing Chung’s disclosure among the factors. As U.S. restrictions on intelligence sharing and visa denials for Korean officials continued, calls grew from both the opposition and within the ruling camp for the two officials to be replaced over their roles in straining the alliance. “The existing policy direction will remain in place,” the chief of staff said when asked whether friction with Washington or questions over the effectiveness of Seoul’s North Korea policy had influenced the reshuffle. Along with the security-related positions, Rep. Han Jun-ho of the DPK was nominated for interior minister, while Kang Yu-jung, the president’s chief spokesperson, was nominated for culture minister. Han, a two-term lawmaker, is a former MBC announcer who served on the DPK’s Supreme Council. Kang Yu-jung worked as a cultural critic and university professor and served on the Assembly’s Culture, Sports, and Tourism Committee before becoming a presidential spokesperson. The education minister position remains vacant after former Minister Choi Kyo-jin resigned Sunday over confusion surrounding measures to prevent cheating on the national college entrance exam. The chief of staff said the presidential office would move quickly to select a successor.

The head of state also spoke about Russian drones violating the airspace of Moldova – more than 80 incidents involving drones and other aerial threats in 2026, each followed by information manipulation. “First, they make people feel unsafe. Then they try to convince them that defending themselves is even more dangerous,” the Moldovan president said. Maia Sandu warned countries preparing for elections that protecting the electoral process must begin well before the campaign. “Elections are the moment when people turn their beliefs, fears and perceptions into decisions. And Russia may have spent years shaping them,” Maia Sandu said. editorialRejections.summary: Operating at the minimum quorum required for the Grand Chamber creates significant procedural risks

editorialRejections.body: "Is the Constitutional Court facing a difficult situation with only 12 judges remaining? Absolutely. Operating at the minimum quorum required for the Grand Chamber creates significant procedural risks. Each judge bears a double responsibility to ensure that consideration of cases does not come to a halt. However, the constitutional justice system should not depend on whether one or two judges are physically able to attend a hearing," he said. According to Horodovenko, before his retirement, the Constitutional Court updated its internal procedures to prevent delays in the reassignment of cases. The Court's ability to hear cases also depends on the timely fulfillment of constitutional obligations by the appointing authorities: the Verkhovna Rada, the Congress of Judges of Ukraine, and the President of Ukraine. "Selection procedures are ongoing, and filling the vacant positions as soon as possible is a matter not only of the Constitutional Court's effectiveness but also of the resilience of the rule of law during wartime," he said. Under the Law of Ukraine "On the Constitutional Court of Ukraine," the Grand Chamber is authorized to consider submissions provided that it has at least 12 judges. The Court's two existing senates are authorized to consider constitutional complaints provided that at least six judges participate. With Horodovenko's nine-year term having expired, the Second Senate is now left with only five judges. Consequently, it has lost the quorum required to consider constitutional complaints. While the Constitutional Court is supposed to have 18 judges, it currently has only 12. Six positions remain vacant. The Court also has neither a Chairperson nor a Deputy Chairperson. As a result, the duties of the Court's Chairperson are being performed by Oleksandr Petryshyn, the senior judge by age. The Advisory Group of Experts is responsible for selecting candidates for Constitutional Court judge positions. It announced that on July 9, 2026, it had submitted documents to the Verkhovna Rada Committee on Legal Policy concerning nine candidates who had passed the assessment for two vacant Constitutional Court positions allocated to Parliament. Ukrinform asked Vasyl Nimchenko, Acting Head of the Verkhovna Rada's Committee on Legal Policy, when Parliament might appoint the two judges. He said that on November 11, the Committee had interviewed nine candidates for the two vacant Constitutional Court positions allocated to Parliament. Following the interviews, eight candidates were recommended for appointment as Constitutional Court judges, while one was not. Nimchenko expressed hope that, following a meeting of the parliamentary conciliation council, the issue of appointing Constitutional Court judges would be placed on Parliament's agenda in the near future. According to the Advisory Group of Experts, two vacancies remain under the quota allocated to the Congress of Judges of Ukraine. The group has completed its assessment of candidates and submitted documents concerning five candidates to the Council of Judges of Ukraine on August 28 this year. The issue of electing two new Constitutional Court judges may be placed on the agenda of the next Congress of Judges of Ukraine. One more Constitutional Court position allocated to the President remains vacant. The competitive selection process for this position is still underway. In addition, applications have opened for candidates seeking to fill one Constitutional Court position allocated to Parliament, which became vacant following Horodovenko's retirement. As Ukrinform reported, on January 27, 2025, the Constitutional Court lost its quorum following the simultaneous retirement of three judges – Viktor Kryvenko, Volodymyr Moisyk, and Viktor Kolisnyk – and was unable to hold hearings of the Grand Chamber and the Second Senate.

editorialRejections.title: Ukrainian Drone Commander Warns NATO Is Training For 'The Wrong War'
editorialRejections.reason: Ukraine coverage requires an international news source
editorialRejections.body: Maj. Olha Bihar, who leads drone units in Ukraine's 20th Army Corps, tells Forces News that tanks can barely operate near the front and that "strength is not about muscles anymore" ERBIL (Kurdistan 24) - Ukrainian Maj. Olha Bihar, known by her call sign "Vidma," or "Witch," warned that NATO forces are still training their soldiers on traditional military concepts that the battlefield has outgrown, saying drones have fundamentally reshaped war. In an interview with Britain's Forces News in London, Bihar, who heads the Unmanned Systems Directorate of the 20th Army Corps of Ukraine's army, said tanks, armored vehicles and conventional equipment have become almost unable to operate near the front because of the dense presence of drones that can detect and strike targets. Bihar said the 15 kilometers nearest the front line have become a kill zone, adding that Ukraine has many tanks, armored vehicles and other equipment but cannot use them because the area has become one of total destruction. She said traditional doctrine and training no longer suit the reality of battle, because drones can destroy classic patterns of fighting and leave soldiers and equipment visible and open to attack around the clock, even when hiding under trees and bushes. Asked whether NATO forces are preparing correctly for future wars, she answered: "No. Definitely not." She called for rethinking military strength, saying "the trend is not about muscles, it's about intellect," and that people armies did not consider fit to fight ten years ago, such as thin young men skilled with computers and video games, are now the ones who can decide the course of battle. She cited the targeting of the Kerch Bridge, which links Crimea to Russia, to show how operations have changed, saying such an operation does not necessarily need a strongly built soldier and "could have been a woman, a skinny gamer, a 50-year-old." Bihar ended by stressing the need to change armies' "frame of thinking" and open up to new ideas in recruitment and training, saying modern wars require technical skills and minds able to handle advanced systems more than traditional physical strength. Ukraine has pursued a 15-kilometer drone "kill zone" along its front, a project known as the Drone Line, and Britain and Denmark are reportedly receiving drone warfare training from Ukrainian instructors, according to the Atlantic Council.

editorialRejections.title: Hungary plans to withdraw its blockade of Ukraine’s EU accession talks
editorialRejections.summary: This opens the possibility for Kyiv and Chisinau to begin negotiations on all membership chapters in the European Union, Euronews reported
editorialRejections.reason: Editor rejected this or a closely matching story
editorialRejections.body: After the long-standing blockade by Budapest, Hungary has agreed to withdraw its objections to the opening of the last two negotiating clusters with Ukraine, diplomatic sources confirmed. This opens the possibility for Kyiv and Chisinau to begin negotiations on all membership chapters in the European Union, Euronews reported. According to two diplomatic sources, Hungary plans to drop the veto at the meeting of the ambassadors of the EU member states. The intention was announced by Andras Biro-Nagy, state secretary for EU affairs, during the debate on enlargement in Brussels. Budapest had long blocked Ukraine’s candidacy, thereby also slowing the progress of Moldova, whose accession process was linked to the Ukrainian one. The change of position comes after Peter Magyar took power from Viktor Orban, who had been at the head of the Hungarian government for 16 years, Skopje1.mk reported. The first negotiating cluster was opened in June, the second in July, and the next two in October. Last month, Kyiv and Budapest reached an agreement on the rights of the Hungarian minority in western Ukraine, which was then adopted in the Ukrainian parliament. Although the Hungarian government announced readiness for the next step, the opening of the last two clusters was postponed for several weeks. Magyar and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy held their first bilateral meeting in Brussels on 16 October, on the margins of the European Council summit, which represented an additional step toward improving relations between the two neighboring countries. Among the clusters that are to be opened are also sensitive areas such as the environment and agriculture. Agriculture in particular will be an especially big challenge for Ukraine. The European Commission, under pressure from countries such as Poland and France, proposed restrictions on the access of certain Ukrainian agricultural products to the European market and EU funds. Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhiy Koretky stated that Kyiv cannot accept the permanent exclusion of Ukrainian farmers from the European market and emphasized that any restrictions must be temporary and proportional. The opening of the negotiating clusters is only the beginning of the accession process. The candidates then have to align their laws and practices with European rules, and the EU member states have more than a hundred opportunities in the further phases to impose a veto and block progress.

editorialRejections.title: Bloodshot eyes and tardiness: When do Kazakh civil servants face drug tests?
editorialRejections.summary: Kazakhstan has approved new rules for identifying signs of drug use among civil servants
editorialRejections.reason: Question headlines are excluded
editorialRejections.body: Kazakhstan has approved new rules for identifying signs of drug use among civil servants. Frequent tardiness, bloodshot eyes, drowsiness and even a loss of interest in work can now serve as grounds for referring a government employee for a medical examination. Under the new rules , civil servants’ behavior during working hours will be monitored by their immediate supervisors and human resources departments. They are instructed to look for three categories of signs that may indicate drug use. The third category concerns mental and cognitive changes. These include memory problems, reduced concentration, anxiety, panic attacks, obsessive thoughts, hallucinations, inconsistent behavior and an inability to critically assess one’s own condition. A single instance of tardiness or bloodshot eyes is not enough to refer a civil servant for a medical examination. Under the order, a referral requires at least three signs of potential drug use from different categories. In such cases, human resources personnel must consider not only the employee’s behavior but also existing information about them, including complaints, performance evaluations, internal memos and other relevant documents. If a supervisor notices suspicious changes in a subordinate’s behavior, they must immediately notify the human resources department. If drug use is confirmed, the head of the government agency must report the findings to the authorized body responsible for civil service affairs and law enforcement agencies. The agency must also consider disciplinary action against the employee. At the same time, civil servants have the right to review their examination results and appeal both the medical conclusion and the actions of government officials. In July 2026, legislative amendments came into force in Kazakhstan requiring drug testing for civil servants. The requirement primarily applies to managers who supervise other employees and civil servants working under special conditions, such as those with access to state secrets. The heads of the respective government agencies are responsible for determining the specific list of positions subject to testing. In March 2026, Kursiv.media also reported on a proposal to classify drug use as conduct that discredits the civil service. Driving under the influence of alcohol or drugs was also designated as an offense that could discredit a civil servant. Additionally, in 2024, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev signed a law prohibiting civil servants from participating in gambling . The ban reportedly affected approximately 280,000 government officials, military personnel and heads of state-funded organizations. For example, in the North Kazakhstan region, nine officials lost their jobs because of gambling addiction. In the Akmola region, civil servants faced disciplinary action for placing bets worth millions of tenge with bookmakers, while gambling-related offenses in the Zhetysu region also resulted in dismissals.

While an excavator was operating, they noticed a pile of construction debris move. They stopped the machinery and began checking the rubble. But then it suddenly moved... It had survived. How? After the explosion, amid the rubble, in thick smoke and dust... No one knows. When it was pulled out, it was already able to get up on its paws. A little miracle that, despite everything, wanted so much to live." Dym was rushed to a veterinary clinic. The animal rescuers took him into their care. What is known about the strike on the apartment block in Dymer, Kyiv Oblast At around 05:00 on 22 November, a Russian drone struck a five-storey residential building, destroying apartments on all five floors and sparking a fire. Residents who survived were evacuated. Emergency workers managed to rescue seven-year-old Davyd, who had been trapped under the building's structural elements for almost 14 hours. They also pulled 79-year-old Valentyna from the rubble. She had spent 22 hours there. Search and rescue operations continued throughout the night. State Emergency Service units, psychologists, sniffer dog handlers and bomb disposal experts were working at the site of the strike. Eleven people are now known to have been killed, including an 18-year-old young man and an 11-year-old child. editorialRejections.title: Libya condemns Ukrainian attack on Russian ship off Benghazi
editorialRejections.body:
Libya's ⁠Tripoli-based government condemned ​on Monday Ukrainian ​military operations targeting Russian naval vessels near the eastern city ​of ‌Benghazi, saying Libya ⁠would not accept being drawn ‌into the Russia-Ukraine conflict.

Responding to Ukrainian ⁠President Volodymyr Zelensky's remarks announcing military operations against ​Russian naval vessels off ‌Benghazi, the Libyan Foreign Ministry said in a statement: "The ‌continuation of the war ​between Russia and Ukraine gives neither side the right to conduct ​military operations on Libyan ​territory or in ​its territorial waters."

It also said ​foreign forces would not be allowed to use Libyan ports and civilian infrastructure ⁠for military purposes.
